PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

An angle is made when two lines meet at a point. In this sub-strand you will find angles made by lines on a chart, spot angles on objects such as cubes and cuboids, and see how the amount of a turn is the same thing as the size of an angle. You will also look at how people use angles every day.

## Strand 3.0: Geometry
Sub-strand 3.2: Angles
Suggested lessons: 5

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify an angle at a point in lines
b) identify angles from the objects in the environment
c) relate a turn to angles in real-life situations
d) appreciate use of angles in real-life situations

## What this sub-strand covers
• Angles at a point
• Relating turns to angles

## Key inquiry questions
1. How can we use angles in daily life?

## Core competencies
• Communication and collaboration: learner collaboratively works with others and recognises angles that are made by 2 lines that meet at a point using a chart with a different line.

## Values
• Responsibility: learner observes safety precautions while identifying angles from objects such as cubes, cuboids in the environment.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Environmental Education: learner explores and identifies angles from objects such as cubes, and cuboids in the environment.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate angles from objects such as cubes and cuboids in the environment to perspective in Creative Arts.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Mathematics Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 3.0 Geometry, Sub-strand 3.2 Angles

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Angles at a point

LESSON 1: ANGLES AT A POINT
===========================

## What you will learn
• Explain what an angle is.
• Identify the angles made where lines meet at a point.
• Recognise a right angle and tell whether an angle is smaller or bigger than a right angle.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify an angle at a point in lines

## Introduction
Open a book a little, then wider, then wider still. The two covers meet along the spine, and the gap between them grows. That opening between two lines that meet is an angle.

## Notes
### What is an angle?
When two straight lines meet at a point, they make an angle. The point where the lines meet is called the vertex. The two lines are called the arms of the angle. The angle is the amount of opening, or turn, between the two arms.

The size of an angle does not depend on how long the arms are. If you draw the same two arms longer, the opening between them stays the same, so the angle is the same.

### Counting angles at a point
- Two lines that meet at their ends, like the letter L or V, make 1 angle.
- A line that meets the middle of another line, like the letter T, makes 2 angles, one on each side.
- Two lines that cross each other, like the letter X or a plus sign +, make 4 angles at the point where they cross.

### The right angle
The corner of a book, the corner of a door and the corner of this page are all the same kind of angle. It is called a right angle, or a square corner. Right angles are often marked with a small square drawn in the corner.

You can make a right angle tester: fold a piece of paper in half, then fold it in half again so the folded edges lie on top of each other. The corner you get is a right angle.

### Comparing angles
Put the corner of your tester on the vertex of an angle with one edge along one arm.

- If the other arm is inside the tester, the angle is smaller than a right angle.
- If the other arm lies exactly along the other edge, it is a right angle.
- If the other arm is outside the tester, the angle is bigger than a right angle.

When two lines cross to make a plus sign, all 4 angles are right angles.

## Key words
• angle — the amount of opening or turn between two lines that meet at a point
• vertex — the point where the two arms of an angle meet
• arms — the two lines that make an angle
• right angle — a square corner, like the corner of a book

## Worked examples

### Example 1
How many angles are made at the point where the two lines of the letter X cross?

Working:
1. The two lines cross and make four openings around the point: top, bottom, left and right.

Answer: 4

### Example 2
How many angles does the letter T make where its lines meet?

Working:
1. The upright line meets the middle of the top line.
2. There is one angle on its left and one on its right.

Answer: 2

### Example 3
Three straight lines cross at one point. How many angles are there at the point?

Working:
1. Each line crossing through the point adds 2 angles, one on each side.
2. 3 lines × 2 = 6

Answer: 6

## Activity: Angles on a line chart
You will need: Chart with different lines meeting at points, Plain paper for a right angle tester, Pencil and ruler
1. In your group, look at the chart. Point to each place where 2 lines meet at a point.
2. Count the angles made at each point and write the number next to it.
3. Fold a piece of paper twice to make a right angle tester.
4. Use the tester to sort each angle on the chart: smaller than a right angle, a right angle, or bigger than a right angle.
5. Draw your own letters L, T, V and X with a ruler and mark the angles in each.

## Practice
1. What is the name of the point where the two arms of an angle meet?
2. How many angles are made where the lines of a plus sign (+) cross?
3. The letter V is drawn with longer arms. Does the angle get bigger?
4. Four straight lines cross at one point. How many angles are there at the point?

## Summary
• An angle is made where two lines meet at a point called the vertex.
• Two crossing lines make 4 angles.
• A right angle is a square corner.

### Answers to practice
1. The vertex
2. 4
3. No. The size of an angle depends on the opening between the arms, not on how long the arms are.
4. 8

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Angles on objects in the environment

LESSON 2: ANGLES ON OBJECTS IN THE ENVIRONMENT
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Identify angles on cubes, cuboids and other objects.
• Count the right angles on the faces of a cube or cuboid.

Curriculum outcomes: b) identify angles from the objects in the environment; d) appreciate use of angles in real-life situations

## Introduction
A box of chalk, a brick, a match box and a dice all have corners. Every corner is a place where edges meet, and wherever edges meet there are angles.

## Notes
Angles are all around us. You can find them wherever two edges or lines meet.

### Cubes and cuboids
A cube is a solid shape like a dice. All its faces are squares of the same size. A cuboid is a solid shape like a box of chalk, a brick or a match box. Its faces are rectangles, and some may be squares.

Cubes and cuboids have:

- 6 flat faces
- 12 edges, where two faces meet
- 8 corners, where three edges meet

### Angles on the faces
Each face of a cube or cuboid has 4 corners, and each corner of the face is a right angle. Check this by putting your right angle tester into the corner of a box.

Since there are 6 faces and each face has 4 right angles, there are 6 × 4 = 24 right angles on the faces of a cube or cuboid.

### Angles in the classroom and at home
- Corners of a door, a window, a desk top, the chalkboard and a book are right angles.
- The two hands of a clock make an angle at the centre of the clock.
- The legs of a folding ladder or an open pair of scissors make angles that can be smaller than a right angle.
- The roof of many houses meets at the top to make an angle.

### Why angles matter
Builders check that walls meet at right angles so that the house stands strong and doors and windows fit. Carpenters make the corners of tables and cupboards square. When a door is opened wider, the angle between the door and the wall becomes bigger.

### Safety
When looking for angles, do not touch sharp corners of metal sheets or broken glass, and ask an adult before climbing to look at a roof.

## Key words
• cube — a solid with 6 equal square faces, like a dice
• cuboid — a solid with 6 rectangular faces, like a box of chalk
• edge — a line where two faces of a solid meet
• face — a flat surface of a solid

## Worked examples

### Example 1
How many right angles are there on all the faces of a match box?

Working:
1. A match box is a cuboid with 6 faces.
2. Each face has 4 right angles.
3. 6 × 4 = 24

Answer: 24

### Example 2
How many right angles are there on the top face of a desk?

Working:
1. The top of a desk is a rectangle.
2. A rectangle has 4 corners, all right angles.

Answer: 4

### Example 3
A class has 3 windows. Each window is a rectangle. How many right angles do the corners of the windows make altogether?

Working:
1. Each window has 4 right angles.
2. 3 × 4 = 12

Answer: 12

## Activity: Angle hunt with cubes and cuboids
You will need: Empty boxes (cuboids), A dice or cube, Right angle tester, Exercise book
1. In your group, hold a box and point to its faces, edges and corners. Count each.
2. Use your right angle tester to check the corners of each face.
3. Count the right angles on all the faces and record the number.
4. Walk safely round the classroom and list 5 other objects that have right angles.
5. Share your list with another group.

## Practice
1. How many faces does a cube have?
2. How many right angles are on 2 faces of a cube?
3. Name two objects in the classroom that have right angles.
4. Why do builders make walls meet at right angles?

## Summary
• Cubes and cuboids have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners.
• Every face of a cube or cuboid has 4 right angles.
• Angles are found wherever edges or lines meet.

### Answers to practice
1. 6
2. 8
3. For example a book, the chalkboard, a desk top, a door or a window.
4. So that the building is strong and doors, windows and roofs fit well.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Relating turns to angles

LESSON 3: RELATING TURNS TO ANGLES
==================================

## What you will learn
• Explain that an angle is an amount of turn.
• Relate quarter, half and full turns to right angles.

Curriculum outcomes: c) relate a turn to angles in real-life situations; d) appreciate use of angles in real-life situations

## Introduction
Stand facing the chalkboard, then make a quarter turn clockwise to face the side wall. The line you were looking along and the new line you are looking along make a square corner at your feet. A turn makes an angle.

## Notes
In Position and Direction you made quarter, half and full turns. Every turn makes an angle between where you started facing and where you end up facing.

### Quarter turn and right angle
A quarter turn makes a right angle. When the minute hand of a clock turns from 12 to 3, the hand at the start and the hand at the end make a right angle at the centre of the clock.

At 3 o'clock the hour hand points to 3 and the minute hand points to 12. The two hands make a right angle. At 9 o'clock they also make a right angle.

### Half turn and a straight line
A half turn is made of two quarter turns, so it is the same as 2 right angles. The start and end make a straight line. At 6 o'clock the two hands of a clock point in opposite directions and make a straight line.

### Full turn
A full turn is made of four quarter turns, so it is the same as 4 right angles. You end facing where you started.

### Turns in daily life
- A door that is opened until it makes a square corner with the wall has turned a quarter turn.
- When you turn a key in a lock, a tap or a steering wheel, you are making an angle.
- A football player who turns to face the opposite goal has made a half turn, which is 2 right angles.
- Road signs show arrows that bend at an angle to tell drivers which way to turn.

The bigger the turn, the bigger the angle. A turn smaller than a quarter turn makes an angle smaller than a right angle.

## Key words
• amount of turn — how far something turns; this is the size of an angle
• straight line — what a half turn makes; it is equal to 2 right angles

## Worked examples

### Example 1
How many right angles are there in a half turn?

Working:
1. A half turn is 2 quarter turns.
2. Each quarter turn is 1 right angle.

Answer: 2

### Example 2
How many right angles are there in a full turn?

Working:
1. A full turn is 4 quarter turns.
2. Each quarter turn is 1 right angle.

Answer: 4

### Example 3
The minute hand turns clockwise from 12 to 9. How many right angles has it turned through?

Working:
1. 12 to 3 is one right angle, 3 to 6 is another, 6 to 9 is another.
2. Each right angle is 3 numbers on the clock: 9 ÷ 3 = 3

Answer: 3 right angles

## Activity: Make turns, make angles
You will need: Open space, Two long sticks or rulers, Paper clock with two hands
1. One learner stands on a point and holds a stick pointing forward. A partner places another stick on the ground along the first direction.
2. The learner makes a clockwise quarter turn and points the stick again. Place the second stick on the ground. Check the angle between the two sticks with a right angle tester.
3. Repeat for a clockwise half turn and see that the sticks make a straight line.
4. On the paper clock, set the hands to 3 o'clock, 6 o'clock and 9 o'clock. Say whether the hands make a right angle or a straight line.

## Practice
1. What angle is made by a quarter turn?
2. At what time between 1 o'clock and 11 o'clock do the two hands of a clock make a straight line?
3. A learner makes 3 quarter turns. How many right angles has she turned through?
4. Give one example from daily life where a turn makes an angle.

## Summary
• An angle is an amount of turn.
• A quarter turn makes a right angle.
• A half turn is 2 right angles and a full turn is 4 right angles.

### Answers to practice
1. A right angle
2. 6 o'clock
3. 3
4. For example opening a door, turning a key, turning a steering wheel or turning to face another direction.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 3.2 ANGLES
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. What is the point where two arms of an angle meet called?
   A. Edge
   B. Vertex
   C. Face
   D. Arm

2. How many angles are made where two straight lines cross?
   A. 1
   B. 2
   C. 3
   D. 4

3. How many angles does the letter L make?
   A. 1
   B. 2
   C. 3
   D. 4

4. Which of these corners is a right angle?
   A. The corner of a book
   B. The tip of a sharpened pencil
   C. The edge of a ball
   D. The point of a thorn

5. How many edges does a cuboid have?
   A. 6
   B. 8
   C. 12
   D. 24

6. How many right angles are there on all the faces of a cube?
   A. 8
   B. 12
   C. 24
   D. 6

7. Which turn makes a right angle?
   A. A quarter turn
   B. A half turn
   C. A full turn
   D. No turn

8. How many right angles make a full turn?

9. At 3 o'clock, what angle do the hands of a clock make?
   A. A straight line
   B. A right angle
   C. No angle
   D. A full turn

10. Why should a builder make the corners of a door frame right angles?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 3.2 ANGLES
========================================

1. B. Vertex
   The vertex is the meeting point of the arms.

2. D. 4
   Crossing lines make 4 angles round the point.

3. A. 1
   The two lines meet at their ends, making one angle.

4. A. The corner of a book
   A book corner is a square corner.

5. C. 12
   A cuboid has 12 edges.

6. C. 24
   6 faces × 4 right angles each = 24.

7. A. A quarter turn
   A quarter turn is the same as one right angle.

8. 4
   A full turn is 4 quarter turns, each a right angle.

9. B. A right angle
   One hand points to 12 and the other to 3, a quarter turn apart.

10. So that the door fits well and closes properly.
   Square corners let doors, windows and walls fit together.

LESSON 3: RELATING TURNS TO ANGLES
==================================

## What you will learn
• Explain that an angle is an amount of turn.
• Relate quarter, half and full turns to right angles.

A full turn is made of four quarter turns, so it is the same as 4 right angles. You end facing where you started.

### Turns in daily life
- A door that is opened until it makes a square corner with the wall has turned a quarter turn.
- When you turn a key in a lock, a tap or a steering wheel, you are making an angle.
- A football player who turns to face the opposite goal has made a half turn, which is 2 right angles.
- Road signs show arrows that bend at an angle to tell drivers which way to turn.

The bigger the turn, the bigger the angle. A turn smaller than a quarter turn makes an angle smaller than a right angle.

## Key words
• amount of turn — how far something turns; this is the size of an angle
• straight line — what a half turn makes; it is equal to 2 right angles

## Worked examples

### Example 1
How many right angles are there in a half turn?

Working:
1. A half turn is 2 quarter turns.
2. Each quarter turn is 1 right angle.

Answer: 2

### Example 2
How many right angles are there in a full turn?

Working:
1. A full turn is 4 quarter turns.
2. Each quarter turn is 1 right angle.

Answer: 4

### Example 3
The minute hand turns clockwise from 12 to 9. How many right angles has it turned through?

Working:
1. 12 to 3 is one right angle, 3 to 6 is another, 6 to 9 is another.
2. Each right angle is 3 numbers on the clock: 9 ÷ 3 = 3

Answer: 3 right angles

## Activity: Make turns, make angles
You will need: Open space, Two long sticks or rulers, Paper clock with two hands
1. One learner stands on a point and holds a stick pointing forward. A partner places another stick on the ground along the first direction.
2. The learner makes a clockwise quarter turn and points the stick again. Place the second stick on the ground. Check the angle between the two sticks with a right angle tester.
3. Repeat for a clockwise half turn and see that the sticks make a straight line.
4. On the paper clock, set the hands to 3 o'clock, 6 o'clock and 9 o'clock. Say whether the hands make a right angle or a straight line.

## Practice
1. What angle is made by a quarter turn?
2. At what time between 1 o'clock and 11 o'clock do the two hands of a clock make a straight line?
3. A learner makes 3 quarter turns. How many right angles has she turned through?
4. Give one example from daily life where a turn makes an angle.

## Summary
• An angle is an amount of turn.
• A quarter turn makes a right angle.
• A half turn is 2 right angles and a full turn is 4 right angles.

### Answers to practice
1. A right angle
2. 6 o'clock
3. 3
4. For example opening a door, turning a key, turning a steering wheel or turning to face another direction.
